items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use unit conversions to convert from one set of units to another.

Content:
For instance, the speed of sound is approximately [MATH: 0.34] kilometers per second. What is this in meters per second? We can find out using the following two steps.

Content:
Step 1: Create a conversion formula.

Content:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.] To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

Content:
We want to replace [MATH: \textrm{km}] with [MATH: \textrm{m}.] To get rid of [MATH: \textrm{km},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{km}] in the denominator so that it cancels out:

Content:
[MATH: \require{cancel}
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{?}{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

Content:
Then, to introduce [MATH: \textrm{m},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{m}] in the numerator:
[MATH: \require{cancel}
\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{km}} }{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\cancel{ \textrm{km} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

Content:
So, our conversion formula is

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{s}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{\textrm{km} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.]

Content:
Step 2: Use the conversion formula.

Content:
Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

Content:
- The speed that we wish to convert is [MATH: 0.34 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}}.]
- There are [MATH: 1\,000] meters per kilometer.

Content:
Applying our conversion formula, we have
[MATH: 0.34(km)/(s)|= 0.34(km)/(s) ⋅ 1000(m)/(km); = (0.34 ⋅ 1000)(km)/(s) ⋅ (m)/(km); = 340(m)/(s).]

Content:
Thus, the speed of sound is [MATH: 340] meters per second.

sections.normalized_html: A guitar string, made of carbon steel, has a linear mass density of [MATH: 3\,950] milligrams per meter. What is the linear mass density in grams per meter?
sections.readable_text: A guitar string, made of carbon steel, has a linear mass density of [MATH: 3\,950] milligrams per meter. What is the linear mass density in grams per meter?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.] To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}]

We want to replace [MATH: \textrm{mg}] with [MATH: \textrm{g}.] To get rid of [MATH: \textrm{mg},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{mg}] in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce [MATH: \textrm{g},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{g}] in the numerator.

[MATH: \require{cancel} \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mg}} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{\cancel{ \textrm{mg} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}]

So, our conversion formula is [MATH: \require{cancel} \dfrac{\textrm{mg} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \textrm{mg} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

  • The density given in the problem statement is [MATH: 3\,950 \, \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}.]

  • There are [MATH: 1\,000] milligrams per gram. Taking the reciprocal, there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1\,000}] grams per milligram.

Applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 3950(mg)/(m)|= 3950(mg)/(m) ⋅ (1)/(1000)(g)/(mg); = (3950 ⋅ (1)/(1000))(mg)/(m) ⋅ (g)/(mg); = 3.95(g)/(m).]

Thus, the linear mass density of the string is [MATH: 3.95\,\textrm{g}/\textrm{m}.]

sections.normalized_html: Sand runs through a sand timer at a rate of [MATH: 120] grams per minute. What is this rate in grams per second?
sections.readable_text: Sand runs through a sand timer at a rate of [MATH: 120] grams per minute. What is this rate in grams per second?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}.] To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}]

We want to replace [MATH: \textrm{min}] with [MATH: \textrm{s}.] To get rid of [MATH: \textrm{min},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{min}] in the numerator so that it cancels out. To introduce [MATH: \textrm{s},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{s}] in the denominator.

[MATH: \require{cancel} \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \cancel{\textrm{min}}}\cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{ \textrm{min} } }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}]

Therefore, our conversion formula is

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \textrm{min}}\cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{min} }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{s}}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

  • The rate given in the problem statement is [MATH: 120 \, \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{min}}.]

  • There are [MATH: 60] seconds per minute. Taking the reciprocal, there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{60}] minutes per second.

Applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 120(g)/(min)|= 120(g)/(min) ⋅ (1)/(60)(min)/(s); = (120 ⋅ (1)/(60))(g)/(min) ⋅ (min)/(s); = 2(g)/(s).]

Thus, the sand runs through the sand timer at a rate of [MATH: 2 \,\textrm{g}/\textrm{s}.]

sections.normalized_html: A peregrine falcon can reach a speed of [MATH: 360] kilometers per hour during flight while diving. What is this speed in meters per second?
sections.readable_text: A peregrine falcon can reach a speed of [MATH: 360] kilometers per hour during flight while diving. What is this speed in meters per second?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{km}] to [MATH: \textrm{m}.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} }{\textrm{hour}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{hour}] into [MATH: \textrm{s}.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} }{ \cancel{\color{red}\textrm{hour}} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\cancel{\color{blue}\textrm{km}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{\color{red}\textrm{hour}} }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

So, our conversion formula is

[MATH: \dfrac{\color{black}\textrm{km} }{ \color{black}\textrm{hour} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\color{black}\textrm{km} } \cdot \dfrac{ \color{black}\textrm{hour} }{ \textrm{s} } = \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}}]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

  • The rate given in the problem statement is [MATH: 360 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{hour}}.]

  • There are [MATH: 1\,000] meters per kilometer.

  • The number of seconds in one hour is given by [MATH: 1hour|= 60minutes; = 60 ⋅ 1minute; = 60 ⋅ 60s; = 3600s.] Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3\,600}] hours per second.

Applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 360(km)/(hour)|= 360(km)/(hour) ⋅ 1000(m)/(km) ⋅ (1)/(3600)(hour)/(s); = (360 ⋅ 1000 ⋅ (1)/(3600))(km)/(hour) ⋅ (m)/(km) ⋅ (hour)/(s); = 100(m)/(s).]

Thus, the speed of the falcon is [MATH: 100] meters per second.

- The speed that we wish to convert is [MATH: 0.34 \, \dfrac{\textrm{km}}{\textrm{s}}.]

Item 2 — Example: Performing a Unit Conversion: Converting a Numerator

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.] To figure out what we need to multiply by, we can set up an equation to help us:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}\cdot\, \dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}]

We want to replace [MATH: \textrm{mg}] with [MATH: \textrm{g}.] To get rid of [MATH: \textrm{mg},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{mg}] in the denominator so that it cancels out. To introduce [MATH: \textrm{g},] we can put [MATH: \textrm{g}] in the numerator.

\dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{mg}} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{\cancel{ \textrm{mg} } } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}]

So, our conversion formula is
[MATH: \require{cancel}
\dfrac{\textrm{mg} }{\textrm{m}}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{g} }{ \textrm{mg} } = \dfrac{\textrm{g}}{\textrm{m}}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The density given in the problem statement is [MATH: 3\,950 \, \dfrac{\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{m}}.]
